title: GLP-1 Drugs Like Ozempic Linked to 30 Percent Lower Breast Cancer Risk in Major Study
excerpt: A University of Pennsylvania study of nearly 112,000 women found that those taking weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy were significantly less likely to develop breast cancer, though researchers caution the findings are observational.
body:
• Women taking GLP-1 drugs had roughly 30% lower odds of developing breast cancer compared to matched non-users, according to a study of nearly 112,000 women published in JCO Oncology Practice.
  • The research, presented at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting, analysed health records from the University of Pennsylvania Health System spanning January 2022 to June 2025.
  • Possible mechanisms include weight loss reducing a known cancer risk factor, GLP-1 drugs' anti-inflammatory properties, and potential direct effects on cancer cell metabolism.
  • A separate December 2025 meta-analysis of 48 randomised trials found no significant cancer risk reduction, highlighting the gap between observational and trial-level evidence.

A Striking Association Emerges

Weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy may offer benefits far beyond the scale. A major observational study from the University of Pennsylvania has found that women taking GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs were about 30% less likely to develop breast cancer than women who were not using them.

The research, published in the journal JCO Oncology Practice and presented at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology Annual Meeting in Chicago, analysed electronic health records from nearly 112,000 women aged 45 to 80 with a body mass index of 25 or above. All had undergone breast imaging at Penn Medicine between January 2022 and June 2025.

Of the study population, 15,264 women — about 14% — had been prescribed a GLP-1 drug prior to their imaging. When compared to the full cohort, GLP-1 users had 35.1% lower odds of a breast cancer diagnosis. In a more rigorous one-to-one matched analysis controlling for age, race, ethnicity, BMI, breast density, and diabetes status, the reduction stood at 30.5%.

"While our study was observational and does not definitively confirm an association between GLP-1 medications and reduced breast cancer incidence, it does add to the growing body of evidence suggesting that it's worth investigating these weight-loss drugs as potential cancer prevention tools."

— Dr. Elizabeth McDonald, University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine

How GLP-1 Drugs Might Reduce Cancer Risk

GLP-1 receptor agonists — a class that includes semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) — work by mimicking the naturally occurring glucagon-like peptide-1 hormone. They regulate blood sugar, decrease appetite, and slow digestion. Originally developed for type 2 diabetes, they have become some of the most widely prescribed medications in the United States.

Researchers identified three plausible pathways through which these drugs could influence cancer risk. First, excess body weight — particularly after menopause — is a well-established risk factor for breast cancer, and the substantial weight loss GLP-1 drugs produce could directly reduce that risk. Second, GLP-1 drugs are known to dampen chronic inflammation, which plays a role in tumour development. Third, the medications may have direct metabolic effects on cancer cell growth pathways, though this remains speculative.

Conflicting Evidence Demands Caution

The Penn findings do not exist in a vacuum. A December 2025 meta-analysis published in a separate journal examined 48 randomised controlled trials involving 94,245 adults who were overweight, obese, or had type 2 diabetes. That study found that GLP-1 drugs had little to no measurable effect on the risk of obesity-associated cancers, including breast cancer.

The disconnect likely reflects methodology differences. Observational studies capture real-world prescribing patterns over longer periods but cannot prove causation. Randomised trials are the gold standard for establishing cause and effect but typically follow patients for only about 70 weeks — potentially too short to detect cancer prevention effects given the years-long timeline of tumour development.

Dr. Kandace McGuire, a breast surgeon at Virginia Commonwealth University who was not involved in either study, noted that patients prescribed GLP-1 drugs should be monitored for far longer, particularly for slow-growing cancers like breast and thyroid tumours.

What It Means for Patients

For the millions of women currently taking or considering GLP-1 medications, the Penn study adds a potential benefit to the ledger but does not change clinical practice. No medical organisation currently recommends these drugs for cancer prevention, and the study did not differentiate between specific GLP-1 medications or durations of use.

Dr. McDonald's team is planning further analyses to examine whether specific drugs, treatment durations, or patient subgroups show stronger associations. For now, the message remains straightforward: regular screening and a healthy lifestyle remain the most evidence-backed approaches to reducing breast cancer risk, with GLP-1 drugs a promising area for future research rather than a proven preventive tool.
